segments.name: HOOK
segments.visual: kinetic: the trough figure lands on the first word, then the day
segments.vo: $95,201. That's where this catalog's cash bottoms out on day 13 days, on a business making 32.3% net. You'd say a margin like that can't run out of money. It can, on a date you can read off a calendar.

segments.name: LET THEM BE WRONG
segments.visual: kinetic: the P&L read in the viewer's own words (a real P&L screenshot replaces this beat when the founder supplies one)
segments.vo: Here's the model. You watch the P&L. Revenue up, margin healthy, net positive, so the business is fine and the bank balance is a lagging copy of the P&L. When cash gets tight it's a surprise, and the explanation is always something else. A big PO. A slow payout. A bad month. It's a fair model, because over a long enough window the P&L and the bank do agree. The trouble is the window. Inside it, the money leaves on one set of dates and comes back on another, and the P&L doesn't carry dates.

segments.name: THE CRACK
segments.visual: waterfall: revenue down to true net for the latest month; then cash_cone: the cone opens from today's balance with the wires as red ticks
segments.data_source: MARGIN.DECOMP on Tarnhollow demo data; cash horizon on Tarnhollow demo data
segments.vo: Here's the demo catalog on screen. Tarnhollow, demo data, 24 products, about $3.5M a year. Last month: $318,632 of sales, $102,864 of true net profit, 32.3% net margin. On the P&L this business is fine. Now the bank. $262,000 on hand today. Inside the next 90 days, the supplier wires already scheduled add up to $345,501. That's more than the cash in the bank, on a business that is profitable every month. The money comes back. The question is when, and whether the balance runs dry on the way.

segments.name: CHAPTER 1 — FIND IT
segments.visual: cash_cone: the wires as ticks; then the lead-time span, the shelf span and the payout lag drawn as brackets under the axis, joined into one bar
segments.data_source: cash horizon on Tarnhollow demo data; MONTE_CARLO.RUN on Tarnhollow demo data for lead time and cover
segments.vo: On screen is the cash cone. 10,000 possible versions of the next 90 days, drawn from what this catalog's demand actually does, with every supplier wire as a red tick. Read it left to right, and find the clocks. First, the wire schedule. 35 wires inside the window. The largest, $23,482, for TH-ENADUT-03, leaves on day 0 days. That's today. Next, how long the goods take to arrive. The typical supplier lead time here is 40 days. For that long the money is gone and there's nothing new to sell. Then the shelf. Once units land they sit until they sell. The tightest product in this catalog, TH-STAMIX-12, has 22 days of cover, and slower products sit longer than that. Last, the payout. The platform holds the sale for a 14 days cycle before it pays you. Now put the clocks in a row. Wire, then lead time, then shelf, then payout. The cash conversion cycle is the length of that row: the days between a dollar leaving for the supplier and the same dollar landing back in the bank. It isn't on the P&L because the P&L has no calendar. It's on this chart, because this chart is nothing but a calendar.

segments.name: CHAPTER 2 — VERIFY IT
segments.visual: cash_cone: the trough marked at day {{min_p5_day}}, the floor line, the fan widening to the right with the ends labelled
segments.data_source: cash horizon on Tarnhollow demo data; cash horizon paths, one-year horizon, Tarnhollow demo data
segments.vo: Now verify it against the cone. The median path's low point is $95,201. The bad paths' low point, the worst day of the unlucky tail, is $95,201, and it arrives on day 13 days. Look where that day sits. It's after the wires have left and before the goods have landed, let alone sold and paid out. That's the cycle showing up as a date. In this run the share of paths that ever runs dry is 0.0%. That's with $262,000 in the bank on day 0 days. Bring the starting balance down toward $95,201 and the same schedule, same margin, same products, starts touching the floor. The margin never changed. Only the balance did, and the dates did the rest. And here's what the cone knows that a spreadsheet doesn't. Products don't sell independently. Across this catalog, demand moves together with a correlation of 0.48, so a slow week is slow for most of the products at once, and the trough is deeper than it would be if each product rolled its own dice. Seen from the other end, after 90 days the top of the cone is $352,682 and the bottom is $322,319. Same plan, same margin. Over a full year that gap opens to $65,320 on dice alone.

segments.name: WHAT IT'S WORTH
segments.visual: newsvendor: the overstocked orders as bars above the economic quantity; then kinetic for the clocks and the shortfall
segments.data_source: NEWSVENDOR on Tarnhollow demo data; risk on Tarnhollow demo data
segments.vo: So what's the number worth? Every day you shorten the cycle is a day less of cash sitting in the gap, and here's what's sitting in the gap on this catalog right now. On the shelf clock, stock ordered past its economic quantity costs $3,874 a month in fees to hold, and there are 13 orders the newsvendor would trim. That's cash parked on a shelf. On the wire clock, the largest wire is $23,482 and it goes out on day 0 days, so it sets the depth of the trough more than any other line on the calendar. On the payout clock, 14 days is fixed by the platform. You can't shorten it. You can stop treating it as instant. And the price of getting this wrong isn't a fee. It's the reorder you can't place because the cash is in transit, and the rank you buy back with ads afterwards. The risk model puts the expected shortfall below plan in a bad period at $38,007, and the worst run of periods at $61,358 of net against an expected $99,365. The cycle is where that shortfall lands.

segments.name: WHAT TO DO
segments.visual: kinetic: the steps landing one at a time; cash_cone with the largest wire split and the trough lifting
segments.data_source: cash horizon on Tarnhollow demo data
segments.vo: This week. First, write the cycle down. Wire date, landing date, first sale, first payout, for your top products, from your own POs and settlement reports. It's a spreadsheet with dates in it, and most operators have never made one. Next, draw the wires. Every scheduled supplier payment inside the next 90 days, on a calendar, against the cash you hold and the payouts you expect. Where the line dips lowest is your own day 13 days. Then move the clocks. Split the largest wire into a deposit and a balance where the supplier allows it. That flattens the trough without touching the margin. Trim the orders the newsvendor flags as overstocked, because that cash comes back onto the calendar. Ask for terms before you ask for growth. Last, hold cash for the trough, not for the month. Fixed costs here are $31,500 a month, and the trough arrives on day 13 days. The right reserve is the trough plus a buffer for the cone's bad tail, not a round number of months.

segments.name: THE HONEST LIMIT
segments.vo: What you can do yourself is the calendar for your top products, and it's worth doing this week. What you can't do by hand is the cone. 10,000 versions of the next 90 days across 24 products with demand that moves together, redrawn every time a wire moves or a payout slips. That's a model, and this is one of the places a bad model is dangerous, because a cone drawn too narrow tells you you're safe. What you can do today is stop reading the margin as a cash forecast. Find your day 13 days. You can build this yourself. If you're doing real volume and want it run with rigor, this is what I do, and I only get paid when it works.
